hook.line: Write two sentences about two people and you will repeat their names until it sounds like a list. Spanish has a small set of words that point back at what you just said, so you can keep a paragraph moving. Today you meet them.
hook.es: Rosa y Hernando eran amigos. Este todavía viene al café.
hook.en: Rosa and Hernando were friends. The latter still comes to the café.

examples.es: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; esta dijo que no tiene tiempo.
examples.en: Tomás spoke with Vale and with Mariana; the latter said she has no time.

examples.es: Rosa y Hernando eran amigos. Este todavía viene al café.
examples.en: Rosa and Hernando were friends. The latter still comes to the café.

examples.es: Tomás tiene un carro y una bicicleta. Esta es nueva y aquel es viejo.
examples.en: Tomás has a car and a bicycle. The latter is new and the former is old.

examples.es: Mariana escribió un artículo sobre el café. Dicho artículo salió el domingo.
examples.en: Mariana wrote an article about the café. The article in question came out on Sunday.

examples.es: El gerente recibió una solicitud. Dicha solicitud llegó ayer.
examples.en: The manager received a request. The request in question arrived yesterday.

examples.es: El plazo termina el viernes. Lo anterior no significa que vayamos a cerrar el café.
examples.en: The deadline ends on Friday. The above does not mean that we are going to close the café.

examples.es: Vale y Mariana viven en el mismo barrio.
examples.en: Vale and Mariana live in the same neighborhood.

rule:
Spanish likes to point back instead of repeating a name.

*Este*, *esta* point to the last thing you named: 'the latter'. *Aquel*, *aquella* point to the one named before: 'the former'. They match the gender of what they point to, so Mariana is *esta* and Hernando is *este*.

*Dicho*, *dicha* + noun means 'the one I just mentioned': *dicho artículo*, *dicha solicitud*. It replaces *el*, so never say *dicho el artículo*. It sounds formal, like writing.

*El mismo*, *la misma*: the same one. The *el* or *la* stays.

*Lo anterior* points back to a whole idea, not one noun. *Esto* and *eso* work too.

English does this with 'the latter' or just repeats the name. In chat you can repeat the name too. In a written text, these words make it flow.
smallPrint: Teachers call this anaphora, a word that refers back to something already said. *Dicho* is used here as a referring adjective.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *este* or *esta* for 'the latter' (Mariana). Type the whole sentence: Tomás spoke with Vale and with Mariana; the latter said she has no time.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; esta dijo que no tiene tiempo.
yourTurn.why: Mariana is a woman, so the pointing word is *esta*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *este* or *esta*. Type the whole sentence: Rosa and Hernando were friends. The latter still comes to the café.
yourTurn.answer: Rosa y Hernando eran amigos. Este todavía viene al café.
yourTurn.why: The last one named is Hernando, so *este*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *dicho* or *dicha*. Type the whole sentence: The manager received a request. The request in question arrived yesterday.
yourTurn.answer: El gerente recibió una solicitud. Dicha solicitud llegó ayer.
yourTurn.why: *Solicitud* is feminine, so *dicha*, and it replaces *la*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: Vale and Mariana live in the same neighborhood.
yourTurn.answer: Vale y Mariana viven en el mismo barrio.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: Tomás has a car and a bicycle. The latter is new.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás tiene un carro y una bicicleta. Esta es nueva.
yourTurn.why: The bicycle was named last and is feminine, so *esta*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change it so that the former (Vale) is the one with no time: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; esta dijo que no tiene tiempo.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; aquella dijo que no tiene tiempo.
yourTurn.why: *Aquella* points to the one named first, and Vale is a woman.

yourTurn.prompt: Type it in Spanish: The deadline ends on Friday. The above does not mean that we are going to close the café.
yourTurn.answer: El plazo termina el viernes. Lo anterior no significa que vayamos a cerrar el café.
yourTurn.why: *Lo anterior* points back at the whole idea, so it is always *lo*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; este dijo que no tiene tiempo.
pitfalls.right: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; esta dijo que no tiene tiempo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Este* has to match the person it points to, and Mariana is *esta*.

pitfalls.wrong: Mariana escribió un artículo. Dicho el artículo salió el domingo.
pitfalls.right: Mariana escribió un artículo. Dicho artículo salió el domingo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Dicho* already does the job of 'the', so *el* does not follow it.

pitfalls.wrong: Vale y Mariana viven en mismo barrio.
pitfalls.right: Vale y Mariana viven en el mismo barrio.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English says 'the same' and Spanish needs the *el* too: *el mismo*.

pitfalls.wrong: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; la última dijo que no tiene tiempo.
pitfalls.right: Tomás habló con Vale y con Mariana; esta dijo que no tiene tiempo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish does not say 'the last one' for 'the latter'; *esta* does the pointing.

personal: Name two people in one sentence, then point back at the second with *este* or *esta*. For example: *Hablé con mi hermano y con mi jefa; esta dijo que sí.*
